newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak crown falls further despite cbank assurance.
newsitem.headline: Slovak crown falls further despite cbank assurance.

text.p: Words of calm by the Slovak central bank on Tuesday failed to stabilise the crown, as a new wave of foreign pressure pushed the currency to the floor of its fluctuation band.
NBS vice-governor Marian Jusko said on Tuesday the central bank considered the crown rate "relatively stable and maintainable at least over the shorter-term."

But the crown still touched record lows of around 7.0 percent on the depreciation side of its mark/dollar basket on Tuesday afternoon despite further indirect central bank (NBS) intervention through fixing stronger than market levels.
Most dealers agreed that foreigners seemed to be ignoring the assurances and continued to take up any offer against the Slovak crown they could get, apparently playing on further depreciation.
"Sentiment is bearish at the moment and everybody expects it to remain so in the near future," said one local dealer.
"The market is still waiting for any foreign player to go against the trend and start buying cheap crowns. (But) foreigners still think they can push it even lower," he added.
Analysts also questioned how long the central bank could continue supporting the crown and ward off speculation.
"The question is how long it (the NBS) can afford fixing the crown stronger than the market," said one Bratislava-based crown trader.

The NBS fixed the crown at 33.228 to the dollar and to 19.580 to the mark, implying a deviation against the basket of -0.67 percent. The crown was trading at around -4.5 percent shortly before fixing.
An estimated $50 million flowed from the NBS's hard currency reserves at Tuesday's fixing to complement local bank hard currency positions.
"Look at their (NBS) hard currency reserves; they cannot sustain such a strong fix for long. In fact they should have moved it and followed the market already today," the trader added.
NBS hard currency reserves totalled $3.452 billion as of May 21, but the central bank is estimated to have used some $500 million in its indirect intervetions through fixing over the last week.
The Czech crown and its Slovak counterpart have been under strong speculative pressure over the past two weeks, mainly from foreign banks preying on the currencies' depreciation.

Speculators have forced the Czech National Bank (NBS) to intervene several times to prop up the ailing currency. The CNB finally set the crown free on Monday night, abolishing its +/- 7.5 percent fluctuation band used for daily fixing.
"Traders with the Slovak crown fear the NBS can do the same as the Czech central bank and this only adds to the bearish sentiment," said one Bratislava-based foreign bank trader.

Local analysts have said Bratislava will have to follow the Czech moves, including devaluation, pointing to the fact that Prague still remained Slovakia's largest trading partner and that Bratislava would risk widening its deficit with the Czechs if the Slovak crown remains strong against the Czech crown.

"Even though the NBS wisely limited access to crown funds and made it expensive for speculators to spark further direct pressure on the crown, the trade relation with Prague remains a strong lever that could pull the Slovak crown down along with the Czechs," one dealer said.
But Jusko strictly rejected such ideas, arguing no extra measures were needed to react to the Czech crown decline, which he said was no threat to the mutual trade.
